As of 257 AM EDT Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: High pressure centered to our north will dominate our 
weather pattern as it slowly drifts eastward this week. Mid/high 
clouds associated with a upper shortwave trough will exit to the 
east early this morning, leaving behind mostly clear skies for the 
next few days. Days will feature ample sunshine and high 
temperatures gradually warming from the upper 50s/mid 60s today to 
the mid/upper 60s on Thursday. The dry airmass, clear skies, and 
light winds will result in chilly nights; patchy frost will develop 
both tonight and Wednesday night as lows drop into the low/mid 30s 
across the Adirondacks and much of central/eastern VT. Upper 30s to 
low 40s are expected elsewhere. 

Clouds start to increase Thursday night and Friday as low pressure 
lifts north/northeastward off the East Coast. There remains 
considerable spread in deterministic and ensemble guidance in just 
how quickly and how far north/northeast this feature and its 
associated precipitation is able to move, but consensus at this time 
is that northern NY and much of VT will remain dry through the day 
Friday. Still, given the continuing differences in model solutions, 
have stayed with the NBM for Friday, which keeps PoPs below 30% and 
limits any mention of showers to our far southeastern VT zones.

KEY MESSAGE 2: An area of weak low pressure currently over the western 
Atlantic along a stalled boundary will intensify later this week as 
a shortwave trough over the Midwest is pushed towards it due to 
strong ridging in southeastern Canada. The net result is this low 
pressure system will become part of a large upper level gyre and be 
steered northward. The question is how far east will it track? 

The latest GEFS shows large spread, although there was a clear shift 
to the west in the 00Z guidance compared to 12 hours ago. Relatedly, 
greatest 24 hour chances of measurable rain in Vermont from this 
ensemble increased from 10-40% to 40-60% and more in line with the 
ECMWF ensemble. Have also noted the ECMWF ensemble had trended a bit 
slower in the latest run compared to the 12Z guidance, but with low 
tracks trending northwestward over the course of the weekend towards 
Long Island. As such, while the consensus idea remains that the 
storm track stays far enough south/east such that our region remains 
on the fringes of the event, chances for some rain continue. The 
higher probabilities of rainfall continue to be found in southern 
and eastern Vermont and dwindle towards the northwest. Chances of 
rain peak in the Saturday afternoon through Sunday afternoon 
timeframe, but there remains a chance of showers as early as Friday 
night. Signals for heavy or excessive rainfall are non-existent, so 
these showers would supply a beneficial rain.

In fact, dry northerly low level flow will support gusty wind 
potential given increasing gradient flow as the low pressure system 
deepens as anticipated. The expected north-northeaster flow appears 
to favor the western Champlain Valley and Upper Valley for the most 
climatologically unusual winds, and with regards to the higher 
terrain, the greater potential for seasonably strong northeasterly 
winds remains in southern portions of the region, most likely 
peaking Saturday morning with potential for 850 millibar winds to 
exceed 40 MPH. 90th percentile winds at summit level would possibly 
approach 55 MPH in the southern Green Mountain areas associated with 
a stronger storm tracking farther west than the consensus, which was 
favored by half of the ECMWF ensemble. 

On the western periphery of the large low pressure area, heights 
will continue to rise, leading to a warming trend with low level 
temperatures becoming slightly warmer than normal (850 millibar 
temperatures 60-70th percentile) by Monday. Hence, plentiful 
sunshine amidst dry and mild conditions could exacerbate the long 
term abnormal dryness and moderate drought conditions in the event 
that little or no rain falls over the weekend.
